video_title: Before You Buy the Dip, Ask These 3 Questions
gist: Brett Rentmester (Windrock) attributes the post-midterm selloff partly to a data center backlash: ~56% of voters called it a major issue, 40 of 41 state ballots went against data centers, and Texas, Georgia and Ohio (~37% of US activity) now have governors signaling pauses. With the semiconductor index falling ~12% on Nov 5, he lays out three pre-dip questions (look-through tech exposure, concentrated positions, blip vs systemic) and flags Anthropic's IPO as the next AI barometer.

themes.theme: Midterms and the data center backlash

insights.claim: Brett Rentmester says voters in the midterms cited cost of living, the war, and the AI data center issue, with almost 56% of voters in an NBC exit poll calling data centers a major issue in their vote.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Data centers have become a mainstream electoral issue, adding political risk to the AI infrastructure buildout.

insights.claim: According to Rentmester, 40 of 41 state ballot measures on data centers ended up unfavorable to data centers.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Local and state-level resistance is broad, raising permitting and timeline risk for data center developers.

insights.claim: Texas, Georgia and Ohio, which host something like 37% of all US data center activity, now all have Democratic governors who have signaled a pause or conditional moratorium on data center buildout, which Rentmester calls the spark for the market selloff.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Concentration of buildout in three newly hostile states is a key risk for data center REITs, neoclouds, power and AI capex beneficiaries.
insights.quote: something like 37% of all data center activity are in those three states

insights.claim: Rentmester argues the AI buildout will not ultimately slow: if Texas pauses it moves to Tennessee, if the US pauses China pushes ahead, and if China slows it goes to satellites in space.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Expect geographic reallocation of data center capacity rather than cancellation; beneficiaries may shift to friendlier states.

insights.claim: Maggie Lake frames the American voter as a new stakeholder in the AI trade that markets had not priced in.
insights.speaker: Maggie Lake (host)
insights.so_what: Political risk premia may need to be added to AI infrastructure valuations.

themes.theme: Selloff mechanics and AI bubble debate

insights.claim: On November 5, two days after the election, the NASDAQ fell 6.4% while the semiconductor index fell roughly double that (about 12%), with some individual names down 20-30% in a day.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Semis carry roughly 2x Nasdaq beta to AI-policy shocks; size semiconductor exposure accordingly.

insights.claim: Rentmester cites Morgan Stanley saying the recent hedge fund deleveraging was one of the biggest unwinds in recent years, amplifying moves beyond fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Forced-deleveraging moves can overshoot fundamentals and create whipsaw entry points.

insights.claim: Rentmester says tech trades at a cheaper forward P/E than the S&P 500 and than defensive sectors like staples, so if AI earnings are durable tech looks cheap, but the bear case mirrors 2000 with peak earnings from a one-time capex bump.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: The central question for AI stocks is earnings durability post-capex, not current multiples.

insights.claim: Rentmester believes AI is in its early innings but that a 2022-style drawdown, when the NASDAQ fell 33%, could recur with tech down 25-35% while the decade-long bull market stays intact.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Position for a possible sharp tech drawdown without abandoning long-term AI exposure.
insights.quote: technology goes down 25 30 35% and yet the bull market is still alive the next decade

insights.claim: Rentmester expects the market to penalize leveraged companies that borrowed to build data centers and rent compute to large AI companies, while sparing strong-balance-sheet players.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Differentiate AI infrastructure names by balance sheet strength; debt-funded compute landlords are most vulnerable.

insights.claim: Rentmester says the overall stock market is expensive by historical measures and, in a 'fourth turning' framework, past tailwinds (falling rates and inflation, low debt/GDP) have become headwinds, raising the odds of a multi-year systemic decline rather than a buyable dip.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Buy-the-dip reflexes may fail in a structurally higher-rate, high-debt regime.

themes.theme: Three questions before buying the dip

insights.claim: Rentmester's first question is to measure aggregate look-through technology exposure across all holdings, since the S&P 500 is near record tech weighting and most investors are far more exposed than they realize.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Index investors already own concentrated AI risk; audit look-through exposure before adding tech on dips.

insights.claim: Rentmester's second question is whether any single position is too large, arguing that favorable long-term capital gains rates should not stop trimming, and noting new real estate opportunity zones next year allow gains to be rolled and tax deferred for six years.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Tax-aware concentration reduction tools are available for investors sitting on large AI winners.

insights.claim: Rentmester's third question is whether the selloff is a blip or a systemic shift, and he advises investors overweight tech to dial exposure down somewhat.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Favors trimming tech overweights rather than adding aggressively on the dip.

insights.claim: Rentmester says his firm told clients to be more cautious from around the SpaceX IPO in summer into the midterms, citing fall seasonality and midterm uncertainty in a polarized environment.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Seasonal and election-cycle caution worked this year; a playbook to revisit in future cycles.

insights.claim: Rentmester recommends stress-testing risk tolerance with realistic scenarios like a 20% drop in a week or a 1968-1982-style decade of no real gains, rather than abstract drawdown questions.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Real purchasing-power stagnation is the underappreciated risk for long-only portfolios.

insights.claim: Rentmester expects rising interest rates and inflation for a prolonged period over the next decade or two, citing the 1970s when stocks roughly broke even in real terms and bonds lost significant purchasing power.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Tilt toward real assets and inflation-resilient holdings; nominal bonds are vulnerable over a long horizon.

insights.claim: Rentmester expects Anthropic's IPO, targeted for mid-November, to proceed or be only slightly delayed, and sees it as the first big AI IPO after SpaceX and a barometer for how markets treat AI, with OpenAI and others on deck.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Anthropic's IPO reception will set the tone for the AI IPO pipeline and sentiment broadly.

insights.claim: Rentmester notes SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic are IPOing at valuations above a trillion dollars and will become major S&P 500 constituents, so passive investors will end up exposed regardless.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Index inclusion of trillion-dollar AI IPOs will further raise passive AI concentration.

insights.claim: Rentmester cautions retail investors against chasing AI IPOs because they rarely get the offer price and early trading is choppy with hot money.
insights.speaker: Brett Rentmester
insights.so_what: Wait for post-IPO volatility to settle before buying new AI listings.
